relations.note: Sobek is explicitly called the son of Neith.
Sobek emerges from her leg and tail, though the maternal interpretation is debated.
Isis summons Sobek to retrieve Horus’s severed hands from the water.
Sobek searches for Horus’s hands and recovers them using a fish-trap.
Re questions and instructs Sobek about the hands, fish-trap, and ritual consequences.
relations.source: Coffin Text 158; Book of the Dead 113

relations.note: Duamutef accompanies Horus in the episode, without clear independent action involving Sobek.
relations.source: Coffin Text 158; Book of the Dead 113

relations.note: Qebehsenuef accompanies Horus in the episode, without clear independent action involving Sobek.
relations.source: Coffin Text 158; Book of the Dead 113

relations.note: Hymnic and Fayum traditions present Sobek as assisting or protecting Osiris.
relations.source: Middle Kingdom hymns and later Fayum material

relations.note: Sobek is fused with the royal falcon god as Sobek-Horus of Shedet.
Sobek is fused with Re as Sobek-Re, acquiring solar and creator attributes.
relations.source: Middle and New Kingdom religious sources

relations.note: Sobek and Renenutet receive joint cult in the Fayum agricultural and royal complex.
Kom Ombo theology makes Hathor Sobek’s consort and joint recipient of offerings.
Khonsu is the son of Sobek and Hathor in the Kom Ombo triad.
Sobek and Haroeris occupy separate but coordinated cultic axes at Kom Ombo.
Tebtunis priests fused the local Sobek form Soknebtunis with Geb.
Greek documents render the composite Soknebtunis-Geb as Soknebtunis-Kronos.
Local cultic compounds combine Sobek with Amun as Amun-Sobek.
